steps.text: We're building a tiny decision tree for braking situations, and we'll pick its first question ourselves. This list names our three features: distance, relative speed, and whether it's a pedestrian.
Here are fourteen rows of data, one per situation. Each row holds those three feature values, so the first row means eight meters away, forty-five kilometers per hour, and yes it's a pedestrian.
This brake list is the answer for each row: a one means the car should brake, a zero means go. It lines up with the rows above.
Now we define a function called gini that measures how mixed a group is. Zero means perfectly pure, all one class, and around a half means a total fifty-fifty coin flip.
First a safety check: if the labels list is empty, there's nothing to measure, so we just return zero.
We compute p1, the fraction of ones in the group, then plug it into the Gini formula. The lower the result, the more one-sided and confident the group is.
We call this the root: the impurity of all fourteen rows before we ask any question. This is our starting point to improve on.
These two prints show a summary at the root, how many brake versus go, and the root's Gini impurity. That tells us how messy things are before splitting.
We start an empty candidates list to collect possible questions. Then we loop over the three features by index, so we test each column in turn.
For the current feature, we grab all its unique values and sort them. These are the spots where a meaningful split could happen.
We walk between each pair of neighboring values and set the threshold halfway between them. Splitting at the midpoint is a fair place to divide the two values.
Now we split the rows: left holds the answers where the feature is at or below the threshold, and right holds those above it. This is the question actually sorting the data.
We calculate the weighted impurity after the split, blending both sides by how many rows each holds. This combined number is exactly what a tree tries to make as small as possible.
We save this candidate: the gain, which is root minus after, plus the feature name, threshold, and both branches. Storing everything lets us rank the questions later.
After trying every split, we pick the candidate with the biggest gain and unpack its details. This is the single best first question for our tree.
We announce the winner and print the actual question, asking whether the chosen feature is at or below its threshold. That's the tree's very first decision.
These lines show how far the impurity dropped after the split and how much information we gained. Bigger gain means a cleaner, more useful question.
Finally we describe each branch: how many brake versus go landed on the left and right, plus each side's own Gini. This shows how well the question separated things.
For extra insight we print the top five questions, sorted by highest gain, showing just the gain, feature, and threshold. It reveals how close the runners-up were.
These comments are your challenges: tweak one row to break a tie, or rerun the search on the impure right branch to find the second question. Do that, and you've built a real decision tree.
We start by importing our tools. We grab random for making fake data, decision trees and random forests from scikit-learn, plus helpers to split our data and measure accuracy.
Here's the plan: we'll build 240 braking situations from a physics rule with some real-world messiness added. Setting the random seed to 12 makes sure everyone gets the exact same data every run.
We create two empty lists, rows for our features and labels for the answers. Then we loop 240 times, using underscore because we don't need the counter itself.
For each situation we make up a distance to the object in metres, a closing speed in kilometres per hour, and randomly decide whether there's a pedestrian, zero or one.

We compute time to collision by dividing distance by speed in metres per second. Then we say brake if that time is under 2.5 seconds, or 3.5 if a pedestrian is present, since we want to brake earlier for people.
Eight percent of the time we flip the label with this line, because the real world is noisy and sometimes the data just disagrees with the rule.
Finally we store this situation's three features into rows and its brake answer into labels, building up our dataset one example at a time.
We name our three features: distance, relative speed, and whether it's a pedestrian. These names will make our tree readable later.
We split the data into training and testing sets, holding back 30 percent for testing. The random state of 42 keeps the split consistent so we can compare fairly.
Now we print a header for a comparison table, then loop over different tree depths. None at the end means no depth limit, letting the tree grow as deep as it wants.
For each depth we train a decision tree on the training data. Limiting max depth controls how complicated the tree is allowed to get.
We measure accuracy on the training data and on the test data separately. The training score shows how well it memorized; the test score shows how well it truly learned.
We print each row nicely aligned, including the gap between train and test accuracy. Watch that gap grow as trees get deeper — that's overfitting appearing before your eyes.
Now the fun part: we train a depth-3 tree and print it out as readable text. Because it's shallow, you can actually follow its yes-no questions and see how it decides to go or brake.
Here we train two more models: one deep tree with no depth limit, and a forest of 200 trees that vote together. The forest is our crowd of decision-makers.
We print the test accuracy for all three: the deep tree, the depth-3 tree, and the 200-tree forest. This lets us compare one overfit tree against a whole voting crowd.
Finally we ask the forest what features it found important. We pair each feature name with its importance, sort them highest first, and print a little bar of hash marks to visualize each one.

These comments are your challenges. First, think about why pedestrian importance is near zero given how we defined braking. Second, try shrinking the forest to 5 trees, then 1, and see where its advantage vanishes.
